title: Exception hierarchies with error codes
idea: A custom exception hierarchy gives each failure its own type under one base class, and each type carries a stable error code that callers map to responses.
points: Domain errors are unchecked so middle layers stay clean; one boundary catches and recovers.
Each subclass carries a code from an `enum`; message text stays free to change.
Wrap low-level checked exceptions in domain ones, passing the original as the cause.
Translate at one boundary: domain codes become HTTP statuses there, nowhere else.

hero.title: A bank timeout becomes a stable code

messages.label: pay 777 cents
messages.note: The client asks to pay. `respond` is the boundary that will build the answer.

messages.label: charge(777)
messages.note: `respond` calls the service. It knows nothing about banks or sockets.

messages.label: send(777)
messages.note: The service calls the gateway, whose `send` declares a checked `IOException`.

messages.label: IOException
messages.note: The bank times out. A low-level checked exception comes back.

messages.label: GatewayDownException
messages.note: The service wraps it in `GatewayDownException` with code `GATEWAY_DOWN`, keeping the cause.

messages.label: 503 GATEWAY_DOWN
messages.note: `respond` catches the base type and reads `code()`. No message text is parsed anywhere.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: A bare `RuntimeException` and a handler that parses its message: one rewording breaks the API.

walk.text: `PaymentGateway` rejects charges over its limit. Its only failure signal is an exception message.
Someone reworded the message. The compiler cannot notice, and no test pinned the text.
The handler matches a message prefix, so the new wording falls through to 500.
Compare the declined line with the expected line: the client sees a server fault.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: An abstract base, `final` subclasses, an `ErrorCode` enum, and one boundary that maps codes.

walk.text: `ErrorCode` is the stable contract. Clients key on the constant names; the enum knows nothing about HTTP.
`PaymentException` is an abstract, unchecked base: middle layers need no `throws`, and the boundary catches it.
Each subclass is `final` and writes its own message. Rewording one cannot change behaviour.
The service wraps the checked `IOException` from the bank and passes it as the cause.
The boundary catches the base type, maps `code()` to a status, and is where c05-t01's recoveries happen.
The 777 case shows the wrapped cause is still there for logs and debugging.

pitfalls: One class per message bloats the hierarchy; add a type only when callers react differently.
Mapping by `getMessage()` breaks when someone rewords it; switch on the code instead.
Renaming or reusing a published code breaks clients; add new codes and keep old ones.

quiz.q: Using the classes above, what does this print?
quiz.why: Java picks the first matching `catch`. `CardDeclinedException` is a `PaymentException`, and an enum prints its constant name, not its status.

takeaway: Type per reaction, stable code per type, translation at one boundary.
